However, this approach has traditionally suffered from lower accuracy, hampered by linguistic diversity and limited model capacity.

To address this, we propose a knowledge distillation method to enhance multilingual translation accuracy. First, we train high-performance individual models for specific language pairs to act as "teachers." Then, we train the unified multilingual "student" model not only on standard training data but also to replicate the outputs of these teacher models. This process transfers refined knowledge into the single multilingual system.

Experiments on IWSLT, WMT, and TED talk datasets confirm our method's effectiveness. We demonstrate that one model can handle many languages—up to 44 in our tests—achieving accuracy comparable to or even surpassing that of the individual specialist models.

input:
We introduce PyTorch Geometric, a library for deep learning on irregularly
structured input data such as graphs, point clouds and manifolds, built upon
PyTorch. In addition to general graph data structures and processing methods,
it contains a variety of recently published methods from the domains of
relational learning and 3D data processing. PyTorch Geometric achieves high
data throughput by leveraging sparse GPU acceleration, by providing dedicated
CUDA kernels and by introducing efficient mini-batch handling for input
examples of different size. In this work, we present the library in detail and
perform a comprehensive comparative study of the implemented methods in
homogeneous evaluation scenarios.
Revise this with your best effort: We present PyTorch Geometric, a deep learning library built on PyTorch for irregularly structured data like graphs, point clouds, and manifolds. It provides general graph data structures and processing tools, along with a collection of recent methods from relational learning and 3D data analysis. The library is optimized for high data throughput, utilizing sparse GPU acceleration through custom CUDA kernels and efficient mini-batch handling for variably-sized inputs. This paper details the library’s architecture and offers a thorough comparative evaluation of the implemented methods under consistent, homogeneous scenarios.

input:
Although variational autoencoders (VAEs) represent a widely influential deep
generative model, many aspects of the underlying energy function remain poorly
understood. In particular, it is commonly believed that Gaussian
encoder/decoder assumptions reduce the effectiveness of VAEs in generating
realistic samples. In this regard, we rigorously analyze the VAE objective,
differentiating situations where this belief is and is not actually true. We
then leverage the corresponding insights to develop a simple VAE enhancement
that requires no additional hyperparameters or sensitive tuning.
Quantitatively, this proposal produces crisp samples and stable FID scores that
are actually competitive with a variety of GAN models, all while retaining
desirable attributes of the original VAE architecture. A shorter version of
this work will appear in the ICLR 2019 conference proceedings (Dai and Wipf,
2019). The code for our model is available at https://github.com/daib13/
TwoStageVAE.
Revise this with your best effort:
While variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a foundational deep generative model, key properties of their underlying energy function remain unclear. A prevalent view holds that the standard Gaussian assumptions for the encoder and decoder limit a VAE’s ability to produce realistic samples. This work provides a rigorous analysis of the VAE objective, precisely delineating when this belief holds and when it does not. Building on these insights, we introduce a straightforward enhancement to the VAE framework that requires no new hyperparameters or delicate tuning. Quantitatively, our method generates sharp samples and achieves stable Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores competitive with several GAN variants, while preserving the VAE’s inherent advantages. A condensed version is published in ICLR 2019 (Dai & Wipf, 2019). Code is available at https://github.com/daib13/TwoStageVAE.

(Word count: 138)

input:
Adversarial training is a training scheme designed to counter adversarial
attacks by augmenting the training dataset with adversarial examples.
Surprisingly, several studies have observed that loss gradients from
adversarially trained DNNs are visually more interpretable than those from
standard DNNs. Although this phenomenon is interesting, there are only few
works that have offered an explanation. In this paper, we attempted to bridge
this gap between adversarial robustness and gradient interpretability. To this
end, we identified that loss gradients from adversarially trained DNNs align
better with human perception because adversarial training restricts gradients
closer to the image manifold. We then demonstrated that adversarial training
causes loss gradients to be quantitatively meaningful. Finally, we showed that
under the adversarial training framework, there exists an empirical trade-off
between test accuracy and loss gradient interpretability and proposed two
potential approaches to resolving this trade-off.
Revise this with your best effort: Adversarial training defends against attacks by augmenting datasets with adversarial examples. Intriguingly, adversarially trained deep neural networks (DNNs) produce loss gradients that are more visually interpretable than those from standard models. While this phenomenon is notable, it remains poorly understood. Our work bridges this gap between adversarial robustness and gradient interpretability. We find that adversarial training restricts gradients closer to the image manifold, thereby aligning them better with human perception. We further demonstrate that these gradients become quantitatively meaningful. Finally, within the adversarial training framework, we reveal an empirical trade-off between test accuracy and gradient interpretability, and propose two potential methods to mitigate this conflict.

In this work we show preliminary results of deep multi-task learning in the
area of computational pathology. We combine 11 tasks ranging from patch-wise
oral cancer classification, one of the most prevalent cancers in the developing
world, to multi-tissue nuclei instance segmentation and classification.
Revise this with your best effort: This study presents initial findings on deep multi-task learning for computational pathology. We integrate 11 diverse tasks, from patch-wise oral cancer classification—a major concern in developing nations—to multi-tissue nuclei instance segmentation and classification.

input:
The principle of compositionality, which enables natural language to
represent complex concepts via a structured combination of simpler ones, allows
us to convey an open-ended set of messages using a limited vocabulary. If
compositionality is indeed a natural property of language, we may expect it to
appear in communication protocols that are created by neural agents in language
games. In this paper, we propose an effective neural iterated learning (NIL)
algorithm that, when applied to interacting neural agents, facilitates the
emergence of a more structured type of language. Indeed, these languages
provide learning speed advantages to neural agents during training, which can
be incrementally amplified via NIL. We provide a probabilistic model of NIL and
an explanation of why the advantage of compositional language exist. Our
experiments confirm our analysis, and also demonstrate that the emerged
languages largely improve the generalizing power of the neural agent
communication.
Revise this with your best effort:
The principle of compositionality allows natural language to express an open-ended range of complex ideas by systematically combining a finite set of simpler elements. If this is a fundamental property of language, we should also observe it arising in the communication protocols developed by neural agents engaged in language games.

This paper introduces an effective neural iterated learning (NIL) algorithm that promotes the emergence of more structured, compositional languages among interacting neural agents. These emergent languages confer a learning speed advantage during training, which NIL can incrementally amplify. We present a probabilistic model of NIL and explain the source of this compositional advantage.

Our experiments confirm this analysis and show that the resulting languages significantly enhance the generalization capability of neural agent communication.

input:
Text generation is ubiquitous in many NLP tasks, from summarization, to
dialogue and machine translation. The dominant parametric approach is based on
locally normalized models which predict one word at a time. While these work
remarkably well, they are plagued by exposure bias due to the greedy nature of
the generation process. In this work, we investigate un-normalized energy-based
models (EBMs) which operate not at the token but at the sequence level. In
order to make training tractable, we first work in the residual of a pretrained
locally normalized language model and second we train using noise contrastive
estimation. Furthermore, since the EBM works at the sequence level, we can
leverage pretrained bi-directional contextual representations, such as BERT and
RoBERTa. Our experiments on two large language modeling datasets show that
residual EBMs yield lower perplexity compared to locally normalized baselines.
Moreover, generation via importance sampling is very efficient and of higher
quality than the baseline models according to human evaluation.
Revise this with your best effort:
Text generation is central to many NLP applications, including summarization, dialogue, and machine translation. The prevailing parametric method relies on locally normalized models that predict words sequentially. Although highly effective, these models suffer from exposure bias due to their greedy, step-by-step generation.

In this work, we explore unnormalized energy-based models (EBMs) that operate at the full sequence level rather than token-by-token. To ensure tractable training, we first define the EBM as a residual component on top of a pretrained local model, and second, we employ noise contrastive estimation. Because EBMs assess entire sequences, we can directly leverage powerful bidirectional representations like BERT and RoBERTa.

Experiments on two large language modeling datasets demonstrate that residual EBMs achieve lower perplexity than locally normalized baselines. Furthermore, generation through importance sampling proves both efficient and—as confirmed by human evaluation—higher in quality than baseline outputs.

input:
We propose an energy-based model (EBM) of protein conformations that operates
at atomic scale. The model is trained solely on crystallized protein data. By
contrast, existing approaches for scoring conformations use energy functions
that incorporate knowledge of physical principles and features that are the
complex product of several decades of research and tuning. To evaluate the
model, we benchmark on the rotamer recovery task, the problem of predicting the
conformation of a side chain from its context within a protein structure, which
has been used to evaluate energy functions for protein design. The model
achieves performance close to that of the Rosetta energy function, a
state-of-the-art method widely used in protein structure prediction and design.
An investigation of the model's outputs and hidden representations finds that
it captures physicochemical properties relevant to protein energy.
Revise this with your best effort: We propose an atomic-scale energy-based model (EBM) for protein conformations, trained exclusively on crystallized protein data. This contrasts with established methods, which rely on energy functions built from decades of research into physical principles and carefully tuned features. For evaluation, we use the rotamer recovery task—predicting a side chain’s conformation from its structural context—a standard benchmark for assessing energy functions in protein design. Our model performs nearly on par with the widely used, state-of-the-art Rosetta energy function. Further analysis of the model’s outputs and internal representations reveals that it successfully captures key physicochemical properties relevant to protein energy.

input:
We prove that the reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) of a deep neural
tangent kernel and the Laplace kernel include the same set of functions, when
both kernels are restricted to the sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Additionally, we
prove that the exponential power kernel with a smaller power (making the kernel
less smooth) leads to a larger RKHS, when it is restricted to the sphere
$\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and when it is defined on the entire $\mathbb{R}^d$.
Revise this with your best effort:
We prove that on the sphere \(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\), the reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) of a deep neural tangent kernel and the Laplace kernel contain identical sets of functions. Furthermore, we show that for the exponential power kernel—both on \(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\) and on all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\)—a smaller power parameter (reducing smoothness) yields a strictly larger RKHS.

*(Word count: 73)*

input:
We study training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with ReLU
activations and introduce exact convex optimization formulations with a
polynomial complexity with respect to the number of data samples, the number of
neurons, and data dimension. More specifically, we develop a convex analytic
framework utilizing semi-infinite duality to obtain equivalent convex
optimization problems for several two- and three-layer CNN architectures. We
first prove that two-layer CNNs can be globally optimized via an $\ell_2$ norm
regularized convex program. We then show that multi-layer circular CNN training
problems with a single ReLU layer are equivalent to an $\ell_1$ regularized
convex program that encourages sparsity in the spectral domain. We also extend
these results to three-layer CNNs with two ReLU layers. Furthermore, we present
extensions of our approach to different pooling methods, which elucidates the
implicit architectural bias as convex regularizers.
Revise this with your best effort:
We introduce exact convex optimization formulations for training Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with ReLU activations. These formulations have polynomial complexity in the number of data samples, neurons, and data dimension. Using a convex analytic framework based on semi-infinite duality, we derive equivalent convex problems for several two- and three-layer CNN architectures.

We first prove that two-layer CNNs can be globally optimized via a convex program regularized by the ℓ₂ norm. For multi-layer circular CNNs with a single ReLU layer, we show training is equivalent to an ℓ₁-regularized convex program that promotes sparsity in the spectral domain. These results are extended to three-layer networks with two ReLU layers. Finally, we generalize the approach to various pooling methods, revealing that the implicit architectural bias corresponds to a convex regularizer.

(Word count: 138)

input:
We propose a new metric space of ReLU activation codes equipped with a
truncated Hamming distance which establishes an isometry between its elements
and polyhedral bodies in the input space which have recently been shown to be
strongly related to safety, robustness, and confidence. This isometry allows
the efficient computation of adjacency relations between the polyhedral bodies.
Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 indicate that information besides accuracy
might be stored in the code space.
Revise this with your best effort:
We introduce a metric space of ReLU activation codes using a truncated Hamming distance. This creates an isometry between the codes and polyhedral regions in the input space, which are linked to model safety, robustness, and confidence. The isometry enables efficient computation of adjacency between these regions. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 suggest the code space may contain information beyond just predictive accuracy.

Word count: 74

input:
This paper introduces the first dataset of satellite images labeled with
forage quality by on-the-ground experts and provides proof of concept for
applying computer vision methods to index-based drought insurance. We also
present the results of a collaborative benchmark tool used to crowdsource an
accurate machine learning model on the dataset. Our methods significantly
outperform the existing technology for an insurance program in Northern Kenya,
suggesting that a computer vision-based approach could substantially benefit
pastoralists, whose exposure to droughts is severe and worsening with climate
change.
Revise this with your best effort: This paper presents the first expert-labeled satellite dataset for forage quality and demonstrates a proof of concept for computer vision in index-based drought insurance. We detail a collaborative benchmark tool that crowdsourced an accurate machine learning model. Our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in a Northern Kenya insurance program. This suggests a computer vision-based system could substantially aid pastoralists, whose severe drought exposure is worsening with climate change.

input:
Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have led to
state-of-the-art results for many European-based translation tasks. However,
despite these advances, there is has been little focus in applying these
methods to African languages. In this paper, we seek to address this gap by
creating an NMT benchmark BLEU score between English and the ten remaining
official languages in South Africa.
Revise this with your best effort: Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have achieved state-of-the-art results for many European languages. Yet, African languages have received little attention. To address this gap, we establish an NMT benchmark by evaluating BLEU scores for translations between English and South Africa's ten other official languages.

input:
With the recent success and popularity of pre-trained language models (LMs)
in natural language processing, there has been a rise in efforts to understand
their inner workings. In line with such interest, we propose a novel method
that assists us in investigating the extent to which pre-trained LMs capture
the syntactic notion of constituency. Our method provides an effective way of
extracting constituency trees from the pre-trained LMs without training. In
addition, we report intriguing findings in the induced trees, including the
fact that pre-trained LMs outperform other approaches in correctly demarcating
adverb phrases in sentences.
Revise this with your best effort: The growing prominence of pre-trained language models (LMs) has spurred significant interest in interpreting their internal mechanisms. Responding to this, we introduce a novel method for probing the degree to which these LMs capture syntactic constituency. Our approach enables the direct extraction of constituency trees from pre-trained LMs, requiring no additional training. Notably, the induced trees reveal that pre-trained LMs surpass other methods in accurately delineating adverb phrases, among other intriguing findings.

input:
Magnitude-based pruning is one of the simplest methods for pruning neural
networks. Despite its simplicity, magnitude-based pruning and its variants
demonstrated remarkable performances for pruning modern architectures. Based on
the observation that magnitude-based pruning indeed minimizes the Frobenius
distortion of a linear operator corresponding to a single layer, we develop a
simple pruning method, coined lookahead pruning, by extending the single layer
optimization to a multi-layer optimization. Our experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms magnitude-based
pruning on various networks, including VGG and ResNet, particularly in the
high-sparsity regime. See https://github.com/alinlab/lookahead_pruning for
codes.
Revise this with your best effort:
Magnitude-based pruning is a simple yet effective technique for compressing neural networks. While it minimizes the Frobenius distortion for an individual layer, we extend this principle to a multi-layer optimization. This leads to our proposed method, lookahead pruning. Experiments show it consistently surpasses standard magnitude-based pruning across networks like VGG and ResNet, especially at high sparsity levels. Code is available at: https://github.com/alinlab/lookahead_pruning.

(Word count: 95)

input:
As the share of renewable energy sources in the present electric energy mix
rises, their intermittence proves to be the biggest challenge to carbon free
electricity generation. To address this challenge, we propose an electricity
pricing agent, which sends price signals to the customers and contributes to
shifting the customer demand to periods of high renewable energy generation. We
propose an implementation of a pricing agent with a reinforcement learning
approach where the environment is represented by the customers, the electricity
generation utilities and the weather conditions.
Revise this with your best effort: As the proportion of renewable energy in the power grid increases, its intermittent nature becomes the primary obstacle to fully carbon-free electricity. To meet this challenge, we propose an electricity pricing agent that sends dynamic price signals to consumers, encouraging them to shift their demand toward periods of high renewable generation. We implement this agent using reinforcement learning, modeling the environment to include consumer behavior, power generation utilities, and weather conditions.

input:
We report our experiments in building a domain-specific Tigrinya-to-English
neural machine translation system. We use transfer learning from other Ge'ez
script languages and report an improvement of 1.3 BLEU points over a classic
neural baseline. We publish our development pipeline as an open-source library
and also provide a demonstration application.
Revise this with your best effort: We present a domain-specific Tigrinya-to-English neural machine translation system. Using transfer learning from related Ge'ez script languages, we achieve a 1.3 BLEU point improvement over a standard baseline. Our development pipeline is released as open-source software, alongside a demonstration application.

input:
Nigerian Pidgin is arguably the most widely spoken language in Nigeria.
Variants of this language are also spoken across West and Central Africa,
making it a very important language. This work aims to establish supervised and
unsupervised neural machine translation (NMT) baselines between English and
Nigerian Pidgin. We implement and compare NMT models with different
tokenization methods, creating a solid foundation for future works.
Revise this with your best effort:
Nigerian Pidgin is one of Nigeria's most widely spoken languages, with variants used across West and Central Africa, underscoring its significant role. This work establishes supervised and unsupervised neural machine translation (NMT) baselines between English and Nigerian Pidgin. We implement and compare NMT models using different tokenization methods, thereby creating a solid foundation for future research.

(Word count: 64)

input:
Estimating grape yield prior to harvest is important to commercial vineyard
production as it informs many vineyard and winery decisions. Currently, the
process of yield estimation is time consuming and varies in its accuracy from
75-90\% depending on the experience of the viticulturist. This paper proposes a
multiple task learning (MTL) convolutional neural network (CNN) approach that
uses images captured by inexpensive smart phones secured in a simple tripod
arrangement. The CNN models use MTL transfer from autoencoders to achieve 85\%
accuracy from image data captured 6 days prior to harvest.
Revise this with your best effort: Accurate grape yield estimates are vital for commercial vineyards, guiding key operational decisions. Current manual methods are labor-intensive and achieve variable accuracy, typically between 75% and 90%, depending on the viticulturist's skill. This paper introduces a more consistent and accessible solution: a multi-task learning (MTL) convolutional neural network (CNN). The system uses images from affordable smartphones mounted on simple tripods. By employing transfer learning from autoencoders, the model attains 85% prediction accuracy using imagery captured just six days before harvest.

input:
Automatic change detection and disaster damage assessment are currently
procedures requiring a huge amount of labor and manual work by satellite
imagery analysts. In the occurrences of natural disasters, timely change
detection can save lives. In this work, we report findings on problem framing,
data processing and training procedures which are specifically helpful for the
task of building damage assessment using the newly released xBD dataset. Our
insights lead to substantial improvement over the xBD baseline models, and we
score among top results on the xView2 challenge leaderboard. We release our
code used for the competition.
Revise this with your best effort:
Automated change detection and disaster damage assessment currently demand extensive manual labor from satellite imagery analysts. During natural disasters, timely detection can save lives. This work presents findings on problem framing, data processing, and training procedures specifically tailored for building damage assessment using the new xBD dataset. Our approach yields substantial improvements over the xBD baseline models, achieving a top score on the xView2 challenge leaderboard. The code for this competition entry is publicly released.

(Word count: 96)

input:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are non-linear dynamic systems. Previous
work believes that RNN may suffer from the phenomenon of chaos, where the
system is sensitive to initial states and unpredictable in the long run. In
this paper, however, we perform a systematic empirical analysis, showing that a
vanilla or long short term memory (LSTM) RNN does not exhibit chaotic behavior
along the training process in real applications such as text generation. Our
findings suggest that future work in this direction should address the other
side of non-linear dynamics for RNN.
Revise this with your best effort:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are nonlinear dynamic systems. Prior research has suggested they may exhibit chaotic behavior—characterized by extreme sensitivity to initial conditions and long-term unpredictability. Through systematic empirical analysis, this paper demonstrates that standard RNNs and LSTMs do not display such chaos during training in practical tasks like text generation. Our results indicate that future studies should instead explore alternative aspects of nonlinear dynamics in RNNs.

Word count: 90

input:
Fine-tuning a pretrained BERT model is the state of the art method for
extractive/abstractive text summarization, in this paper we showcase how this
fine-tuning method can be applied to the Arabic language to both construct the
first documented model for abstractive Arabic text summarization and show its
performance in Arabic extractive summarization. Our model works with
multilingual BERT (as Arabic language does not have a pretrained BERT of its
own). We show its performance in English corpus first before applying it to
Arabic corpora in both extractive and abstractive tasks.
Revise this with your best effort:
Fine-tuning a multilingual BERT model represents the current state of the art for text summarization. This paper demonstrates the application of this method to Arabic, which lacks a dedicated monolingual BERT. We present the first documented model for abstractive Arabic summarization and also evaluate its performance on extractive tasks. The model's efficacy is first validated on an English corpus before being applied to Arabic datasets for both abstractive and extractive summarization.

(Word count: 81)

input:
During cluster analysis domain experts and visual analysis are frequently
relied on to identify the optimal clustering structure. This process tends to
be adhoc, subjective and difficult to reproduce. This work shows how competency
questions can be used to formalise expert knowledge and application
requirements for context specific evaluation of a clustering application in the
residential energy consumption sector.
Revise this with your best effort: In cluster analysis, domain experts and visual inspection are often used to determine the best clustering structure—a process that is typically ad hoc, subjective, and hard to reproduce. This work demonstrates how competency questions can formalize expert knowledge and application needs, enabling a context-specific evaluation for a residential energy consumption clustering application.

input:
Action and observation delays commonly occur in many Reinforcement Learning
applications, such as remote control scenarios. We study the anatomy of
randomly delayed environments, and show that partially resampling trajectory
fragments in hindsight allows for off-policy multi-step value estimation. We
apply this principle to derive Delay-Correcting Actor-Critic (DCAC), an
algorithm based on Soft Actor-Critic with significantly better performance in
environments with delays. This is shown theoretically and also demonstrated
practically on a delay-augmented version of the MuJoCo continuous control
benchmark.
Revise this with your best effort:
Action and observation delays are common in real-world Reinforcement Learning, such as remote control. We analyze randomly delayed environments and demonstrate that partially resampling past trajectory fragments enables accurate off-policy multi-step value estimation. Applying this insight, we derive Delay-Correcting Actor-Critic (DCAC), an algorithm based on Soft Actor-Critic. DCAC achieves significantly better performance in delayed settings, a result we prove theoretically and validate empirically on a delayed version of the MuJoCo continuous control benchmark.

(Word count: 80)

input:
We demonstrate that differentially private machine learning has not yet
reached its "AlexNet moment" on many canonical vision tasks: linear models
trained on handcrafted features significantly outperform end-to-end deep neural
networks for moderate privacy budgets. To exceed the performance of handcrafted
features, we show that private learning requires either much more private data,
or access to features learned on public data from a similar domain. Our work
introduces simple yet strong baselines for differentially private learning that
can inform the evaluation of future progress in this area.
Revise this with your best effort: Our findings show that differentially private machine learning has not yet achieved its breakthrough "AlexNet moment" on standard vision tasks. For moderate privacy budgets, linear models using handcrafted features still surpass end-to-end deep neural networks. To outperform these handcrafted features, private learning needs substantially more private data or access to relevant public data features. This work establishes simple, strong baselines to better guide and evaluate future progress in private learning.

input:
Anomaly detection, finding patterns that substantially deviate from those
seen previously, is one of the fundamental problems of artificial intelligence.
Recently, classification-based methods were shown to achieve superior results
on this task. In this work, we present a unifying view and propose an open-set
method, GOAD, to relax current generalization assumptions. Furthermore, we
extend the applicability of transformation-based methods to non-image data
using random affine transformations. Our method is shown to obtain
state-of-the-art accuracy and is applicable to broad data types. The strong
performance of our method is extensively validated on multiple datasets from
different domains.
Revise this with your best effort:
Anomaly detection, which identifies patterns that significantly deviate from the norm, is a core challenge in artificial intelligence. While recent classification-based approaches have shown superior results, they often rely on restrictive assumptions. This work introduces a unifying perspective and proposes GOAD, an open-set method that relaxes these generalization constraints. We also extend transformation-based techniques to non-image data via random affine transformations. Demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy, our broadly applicable method is rigorously validated across multiple datasets from diverse domains.

(Word count: 96)

input:
In this paper, we cast fair machine learning as invariant machine learning.
We first formulate a version of individual fairness that enforces invariance on
certain sensitive sets. We then design a transport-based regularizer that
enforces this version of individual fairness and develop an algorithm to
minimize the regularizer efficiently. Our theoretical results guarantee the
proposed approach trains certifiably fair ML models. Finally, in the
experimental studies we demonstrate improved fairness metrics in comparison to
several recent fair training procedures on three ML tasks that are susceptible
to algorithmic bias.
Revise this with your best effort:
This paper reframes fair machine learning as a problem of invariance. We introduce a formulation of individual fairness that requires model predictions to remain invariant within specified sensitive groups. To enforce this, we design a transport-based regularizer and develop an efficient algorithm for its optimization. Theoretically, our approach guarantees the training of certifiably fair models. Empirically, we demonstrate improved fairness metrics over recent methods across three machine learning tasks prone to algorithmic bias.

(Word count: 89)

input:
Despite significant advances, continual learning models still suffer from
catastrophic forgetting when exposed to incrementally available data from
non-stationary distributions. Rehearsal approaches alleviate the problem by
maintaining and replaying a small episodic memory of previous samples, often
implemented as an array of independent memory slots. In this work, we propose
to augment such an array with a learnable random graph that captures pairwise
similarities between its samples, and use it not only to learn new tasks but
also to guard against forgetting. Empirical results on several benchmark
datasets show that our model consistently outperforms recently proposed
baselines for task-free continual learning.
Revise this with your best effort: Despite notable progress, continual learning models remain prone to catastrophic forgetting when processing sequential data from shifting distributions. Rehearsal methods counter this by storing and replaying a compact episodic memory, typically structured as a set of independent slots. We enhance this framework by introducing a learnable random graph that models pairwise relationships between stored samples. This graph aids both in acquiring new knowledge and in actively preserving past learning. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reliably surpasses recent baselines in task-free continual learning.

input:
We provide a general self-attention formulation to impose group equivariance
to arbitrary symmetry groups. This is achieved by defining positional encodings
that are invariant to the action of the group considered. Since the group acts
on the positional encoding directly, group equivariant self-attention networks
(GSA-Nets) are steerable by nature. Our experiments on vision benchmarks
demonstrate consistent improvements of GSA-Nets over non-equivariant
self-attention networks.
Revise this with your best effort: We introduce a general method for constructing group-equivariant self-attention networks (GSA-Nets) for any symmetry group. The key is to use positional encodings that are invariant under the group's action. This design inherently makes the networks steerable. Evaluations on standard vision benchmarks show that GSA-Nets consistently outperform non-equivariant self-attention models.

input:
We propose to study the problem of few shot graph classification in graph
neural networks (GNNs) to recognize unseen classes, given limited labeled graph
examples. Despite several interesting GNN variants being proposed recently for
node and graph classification tasks, when faced with scarce labeled examples in
the few shot setting, these GNNs exhibit significant loss in classification
performance. Here, we present an approach where a probability measure is
assigned to each graph based on the spectrum of the graphs normalized
Laplacian. This enables us to accordingly cluster the graph base labels
associated with each graph into super classes, where the Lp Wasserstein
distance serves as our underlying distance metric. Subsequently, a super graph
constructed based on the super classes is then fed to our proposed GNN
framework which exploits the latent inter class relationships made explicit by
the super graph to achieve better class label separation among the graphs. We
conduct exhaustive empirical evaluations of our proposed method and show that
it outperforms both the adaptation of state of the art graph classification
methods to few shot scenario and our naive baseline GNNs. Additionally, we also
extend and study the behavior of our method to semi supervised and active
learning scenarios.
Revise this with your best effort: We propose a study on few-shot graph classification using graph neural networks (GNNs), aiming to recognize unseen classes from only a limited set of labeled graph examples. Although recent GNN variants show promise for standard node and graph classification, their performance degrades significantly when labeled data is scarce in the few-shot setting. To address this, we introduce an approach that assigns a probability measure to each graph derived from the spectrum of its normalized Laplacian matrix. Using the Lp Wasserstein distance as our metric, we cluster the original graph labels into broader “super-classes” based on these spectral measures. A super-graph is then constructed to explicitly represent relationships among these super-classes. This super-graph is fed into our novel GNN framework, which leverages these latent inter-class connections to achieve superior separation between graph class labels. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our method outperforms both state-of-the-art graph classification models adapted to the few-shot scenario and naive GNN baselines. Furthermore, we extend and analyze the behavior of our approach in semi-supervised and active learning scenarios.

input:
In this work, we investigate the positional encoding methods used in language
pre-training (e.g., BERT) and identify several problems in the existing
formulations. First, we show that in the absolute positional encoding, the
addition operation applied on positional embeddings and word embeddings brings
mixed correlations between the two heterogeneous information resources. It may
bring unnecessary randomness in the attention and further limit the
expressiveness of the model. Second, we question whether treating the position
of the symbol \texttt{[CLS]} the same as other words is a reasonable design,
considering its special role (the representation of the entire sentence) in the
downstream tasks. Motivated from above analysis, we propose a new positional
encoding method called \textbf{T}ransformer with \textbf{U}ntied
\textbf{P}ositional \textbf{E}ncoding (TUPE). In the self-attention module,
TUPE computes the word contextual correlation and positional correlation
separately with different parameterizations and then adds them together. This
design removes the mixed and noisy correlations over heterogeneous embeddings
and offers more expressiveness by using different projection matrices.
Furthermore, TUPE unties the \texttt{[CLS]} symbol from other positions, making
it easier to capture information from all positions. Extensive experiments and
ablation studies on GLUE benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of the
proposed method. Codes and models are released at
https://github.com/guolinke/TUPE.
Revise this with your best effort:
In this work, we examine positional encoding methods in language pre-training models like BERT and identify key shortcomings in existing approaches. First, we demonstrate that absolute positional encoding, which adds positional and word embeddings, creates entangled correlations between these two distinct information sources. This introduces unnecessary noise into attention mechanisms and can constrain the model’s expressive power. Second, we argue that treating the special \texttt{[CLS]} token—central to sentence representation in downstream tasks—the same as other word positions is a questionable design choice.

Motivated by these insights, we propose a novel method: **T**ransformer with **U**ntied **P**ositional **E**ncoding (TUPE). Within the self-attention module, TUPE separately computes word-contextual correlations and positional correlations using distinct parameter sets, then combines the results. This design eliminates noisy interactions between heterogeneous embeddings and enhances expressiveness through separate projection matrices. Additionally, TUPE decouples the \texttt{[CLS]} position from all others, allowing it to more effectively aggregate information across the sequence.

Extensive experiments and ablation studies on the GLUE benchmark confirm the effectiveness of TUPE. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/guolinke/TUPE.

input:
Interpretation of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) training as an optimal control
problem with nonlinear dynamical systems has received considerable attention
recently, yet the algorithmic development remains relatively limited. In this
work, we make an attempt along this line by reformulating the training
procedure from the trajectory optimization perspective. We first show that most
widely-used algorithms for training DNNs can be linked to the Differential
Dynamic Programming (DDP), a celebrated second-order method rooted in the
Approximate Dynamic Programming. In this vein, we propose a new class of
optimizer, DDP Neural Optimizer (DDPNOpt), for training feedforward and
convolution networks. DDPNOpt features layer-wise feedback policies which
improve convergence and reduce sensitivity to hyper-parameter over existing
methods. It outperforms other optimal-control inspired training methods in both
convergence and complexity, and is competitive against state-of-the-art first
and second order methods. We also observe DDPNOpt has surprising benefit in
preventing gradient vanishing. Our work opens up new avenues for principled
algorithmic design built upon the optimal control theory.
Revise this with your best effort: Viewing Deep Neural Network (DNN) training as an optimal control problem for nonlinear dynamical systems has gained significant interest, but progress in algorithms has been modest. This work advances that direction by reframing training through the lens of trajectory optimization. We first demonstrate that widely-used DNN training algorithms have fundamental connections to Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP), a renowned second-order technique from Approximate Dynamic Programming. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel optimizer class, the DDP Neural Optimizer (DDPNOpt), designed for feedforward and convolutional networks. DDPNOpt employs layer-wise feedback policies, enhancing convergence and decreasing sensitivity to hyperparameters compared to existing approaches. It surpasses other optimal-control-based methods in convergence speed and complexity, and proves competitive with state-of-the-art first and second-order optimizers. Additionally, we find DDPNOpt offers a surprising advantage in mitigating vanishing gradients. This research establishes a foundation for new, principled algorithmic designs grounded in optimal control theory.

input:
In this paper, we investigate the effects of releasing arXiv preprints of
papers that are undergoing a double-blind review process. In particular, we ask
the following research question: What is the relation between de-anonymization
of authors through arXiv preprints and acceptance of a research paper at a
(nominally) double-blind venue? Under two conditions: papers that are released
on arXiv before the review phase and papers that are not, we examine the
correlation between the reputation of their authors with the review scores and
acceptance decisions. By analyzing a dataset of ICLR 2020 and ICLR 2019
submissions (n=5050), we find statistically significant evidence of positive
correlation between percentage acceptance and papers with high reputation
released on arXiv. In order to understand this observed association better, we
perform additional analyses based on self-specified confidence scores of
reviewers and observe that less confident reviewers are more likely to assign
high review scores to papers with well known authors and low review scores to
papers with less known authors, where reputation is quantified in terms of
number of Google Scholar citations. We emphasize upfront that our results are
purely correlational and we neither can nor intend to make any causal claims. A
blog post accompanying the paper and our scraping code will be linked in the
project website https://sites.google.com/view/deanon-arxiv/home
Revise this with your best effort:
This study examines the impact of releasing arXiv preprints on the double-blind peer review process. Specifically, it investigates the relationship between author de-anonymization via arXiv and the likelihood of paper acceptance at a nominally double-blind conference. The core research question is: How does the posting of preprints before review correlate with acceptance rates, particularly for authors of differing reputations?

Analyzing submissions to ICLR 2019 and 2020 (n=5,050), we compare papers posted to arXiv prior to review against those that were not. We measure author reputation by their Google Scholar citation count. The analysis reveals a statistically significant positive correlation: papers by high-reputation authors that were posted on arXiv were accepted at a higher rate.

To explore this association, we conducted further analysis using reviewers' self-reported confidence scores. The results indicate that less confident reviewers tend to assign higher scores to papers by well-known authors and lower scores to those by less-known authors.

We explicitly state that our findings are correlational; we cannot and do not make causal claims about bias. All scraping code and an accompanying blog post are available on the project website: https://sites.google.com/view/deanon-arxiv/home.

(Word count: 197)

input:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved impressive performance in a variety
of online settings in which an agent's ability to query the environment for
transitions and rewards is effectively unlimited. However, in many practical
applications, the situation is reversed: an agent may have access to large
amounts of undirected offline experience data, while access to the online
environment is severely limited. In this work, we focus on this offline
setting. Our main insight is that, when presented with offline data composed of
a variety of behaviors, an effective way to leverage this data is to extract a
continuous space of recurring and temporally extended primitive behaviors
before using these primitives for downstream task learning. Primitives
extracted in this way serve two purposes: they delineate the behaviors that are
supported by the data from those that are not, making them useful for avoiding
distributional shift in offline RL; and they provide a degree of temporal
abstraction, which reduces the effective horizon yielding better learning in
theory, and improved offline RL in practice. In addition to benefiting offline
policy optimization, we show that performing offline primitive learning in this
way can also be leveraged for improving few-shot imitation learning as well as
exploration and transfer in online RL on a variety of benchmark domains.
Visualizations are available at https://sites.google.com/view/opal-iclr
Revise this with your best effort:
Reinforcement learning (RL) excels in online settings where agents can query the environment freely. Yet, many real-world applications present the opposite scenario: abundant offline experience data is available, while direct online interaction is severely restricted. This work focuses on such offline settings. Our core insight is that when offline data contains diverse behaviors, an effective strategy is to first extract a continuous space of recurring, temporally extended primitive behaviors before using them for downstream task learning.

These learned primitives serve two key functions. First, they clarify which behaviors are supported by the data and which are not, thereby helping to prevent the distributional shift common in offline RL. Second, they provide temporal abstraction, shortening the effective planning horizon. This yields both theoretical benefits for learning and practical improvements in offline RL performance.

Beyond enhancing offline policy optimization, we demonstrate that this primitive learning approach also improves few-shot imitation learning. Furthermore, it aids exploration and transfer when fine-tuning with limited online RL across various benchmark domains. For visualizations, please visit: https://sites.google.com/view/opal-iclr

input:
Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and its variants are mainstream methods for
training deep networks in practice. SGD is known to find a flat minimum that
often generalizes well. However, it is mathematically unclear how deep learning
can select a flat minimum among so many minima. To answer the question
quantitatively, we develop a density diffusion theory (DDT) to reveal how
minima selection quantitatively depends on the minima sharpness and the
hyperparameters. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to
theoretically and empirically prove that, benefited from the Hessian-dependent
covariance of stochastic gradient noise, SGD favors flat minima exponentially
more than sharp minima, while Gradient Descent (GD) with injected white noise
favors flat minima only polynomially more than sharp minima. We also reveal
that either a small learning rate or large-batch training requires
exponentially many iterations to escape from minima in terms of the ratio of
the batch size and learning rate. Thus, large-batch training cannot search flat
minima efficiently in a realistic computational time.
Revise this with your best effort:
Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and its variants are the dominant methods for training deep neural networks. Empirically, SGD is known to converge to flat minima, which typically generalize well. Yet, a fundamental theoretical puzzle remains: how does deep learning, amidst countless possible minima, consistently select flat ones?

To address this quantitatively, we develop a Density Diffusion Theory (DDT). This framework clarifies how minima selection depends precisely on sharpness and training hyperparameters. Our key finding, supported both theoretically and empirically, is that SGD exhibits an *exponential* bias toward flat minima over sharp ones. This strong preference stems from the Hessian-dependent covariance structure of its inherent gradient noise. In contrast, Gradient Descent (GD) with simple isotropic noise shows only a *polynomial* preference.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that a small learning rate or large batch size causes the time to escape minima to grow exponentially with the ratio of batch size to learning rate. Consequently, large-batch training becomes inefficient, as it cannot explore flat minima within practical computational limits.

input:
The Receptive Field (RF) size has been one of the most important factors for
One Dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (1D-CNNs) on time series
classification tasks. Large efforts have been taken to choose the appropriate
size because it has a huge influence on the performance and differs
significantly for each dataset. In this paper, we propose an Omni-Scale block
(OS-block) for 1D-CNNs, where the kernel sizes are decided by a simple and
universal rule. Particularly, it is a set of kernel sizes that can efficiently
cover the best RF size across different datasets via consisting of multiple
prime numbers according to the length of the time series. The experiment result
shows that models with the OS-block can achieve a similar performance as models
with the searched optimal RF size and due to the strong optimal RF size capture
ability, simple 1D-CNN models with OS-block achieves the state-of-the-art
performance on four time series benchmarks, including both univariate and
multivariate data from multiple domains. Comprehensive analysis and discussions
shed light on why the OS-block can capture optimal RF sizes across different
datasets. Code available [https://github.com/Wensi-Tang/OS-CNN]
Revise this with your best effort: The Receptive Field (RF) size is a critical factor for One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (1D-CNNs) in time series classification. Performance is highly sensitive to this setting, yet the optimal RF size varies substantially across datasets, necessitating significant effort for its selection. This paper introduces an Omni-Scale block (OS-block) for 1D-CNNs, which determines kernel sizes through a simple, universal rule. The block employs a set of kernel sizes, derived from prime numbers based on the time series length, to efficiently cover the optimal RF across diverse datasets. Experiments demonstrate that models using the OS-block match the performance of those with meticulously searched optimal RF sizes. Furthermore, by robustly capturing optimal RFs, simple 1D-CNN models equipped with the OS-block achieve state-of-the-art results on four time series benchmarks, encompassing both univariate and multivariate data from various domains. Comprehensive analyses elucidate the block's ability to adapt to dataset-specific RF requirements. Code is available at https://github.com/Wensi-Tang/OS-CNN.

input:
Welcome to WeaSuL 2021, the First Workshop on Weakly Supervised Learning,
co-located with ICLR 2021. In this workshop, we want to advance theory, methods
and tools for allowing experts to express prior coded knowledge for automatic
data annotations that can be used to train arbitrary deep neural networks for
prediction. The ICLR 2021 Workshop on Weak Supervision aims at advancing
methods that help modern machine-learning methods to generalize from knowledge
provided by experts, in interaction with observable (unlabeled) data. In total,
15 papers were accepted. All the accepted contributions are listed in these
Proceedings.
Revise this with your best effort:
Welcome to WeaSuL 2021, the First Workshop on Weakly Supervised Learning, held in conjunction with ICLR 2021. This workshop aims to advance the theory, methods, and tools that enable experts to encode prior knowledge for automatic data annotation. This annotated data can then train deep neural networks for predictive tasks. The goal is to improve how modern machine learning generalizes from expert knowledge in conjunction with unlabeled data. These Proceedings contain all 15 accepted papers presented at the workshop.

(Word count: 94)

input:
Generative modeling has been used frequently in synthetic data generation.
Fairness and privacy are two big concerns for synthetic data. Although Recent
GAN [\cite{goodfellow2014generative}] based methods show good results in
preserving privacy, the generated data may be more biased. At the same time,
these methods require high computation resources. In this work, we design a
fast, fair, flexible and private data generation method. We show the
effectiveness of our method theoretically and empirically. We show that models
trained on data generated by the proposed method can perform well (in inference
stage) on real application scenarios.
Revise this with your best effort: Generative modeling is widely employed for synthetic data creation, yet fairness and privacy remain significant challenges. While recent GAN-based approaches [\cite{goodfellow2014generative}] effectively preserve privacy, they often amplify bias and demand substantial computational resources. This work introduces a fast, fair, flexible, and private data generation method. We demonstrate its effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and empirical validation. Furthermore, models trained on our synthetic data perform robustly in real-world inference scenarios, confirming the method's practical utility.

input:
Learning from a limited number of samples is challenging since the learned
model can easily become overfitted based on the biased distribution formed by
only a few training examples. In this paper, we calibrate the distribution of
these few-sample classes by transferring statistics from the classes with
sufficient examples, then an adequate number of examples can be sampled from
the calibrated distribution to expand the inputs to the classifier. We assume
every dimension in the feature representation follows a Gaussian distribution
so that the mean and the variance of the distribution can borrow from that of
similar classes whose statistics are better estimated with an adequate number
of samples. Our method can be built on top of off-the-shelf pretrained feature
extractors and classification models without extra parameters. We show that a
simple logistic regression classifier trained using the features sampled from
our calibrated distribution can outperform the state-of-the-art accuracy on two
datasets (~5% improvement on miniImageNet compared to the next best). The
visualization of these generated features demonstrates that our calibrated
distribution is an accurate estimation.
Revise this with your best effort:
Learning from only a few examples is difficult, as models tend to overfit to the biased distribution of a small dataset. To address this, we calibrate the distribution of these few-sample classes by transferring statistical insights from classes with abundant data. From this calibrated distribution, we can then sample a sufficient number of synthetic examples to augment the classifier’s training set.

We model each dimension of the feature representation as following a Gaussian distribution. This allows us to borrow the more reliably estimated mean and variance from similar, well-represented classes to refine the statistics of under-represented ones. Our approach integrates seamlessly with standard pretrained feature extractors and classifiers, requiring no additional parameters.

Experiments show that a simple logistic regression classifier, trained on features sampled from our calibrated distributions, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. This includes an improvement of approximately 5% on miniImageNet over the next best method. Visualizations of the generated features confirm that our method provides an accurate estimation of the true class distributions.

input:
Hopfield networks (HNs) and Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are two
important models at the interface of statistical physics, machine learning, and
neuroscience. Recently, there has been interest in the relationship between HNs
and RBMs, due to their similarity under the statistical mechanics formalism. An
exact mapping between HNs and RBMs has been previously noted for the special
case of orthogonal (uncorrelated) encoded patterns. We present here an exact
mapping in the case of correlated pattern HNs, which are more broadly
applicable to existing datasets. Specifically, we show that any HN with $N$
binary variables and $p<N$ arbitrary binary patterns can be transformed into an
RBM with $N$ binary visible variables and $p$ gaussian hidden variables. We
outline the conditions under which the reverse mapping exists, and conduct
experiments on the MNIST dataset which suggest the mapping provides a useful
initialization to the RBM weights. We discuss extensions, the potential
importance of this correspondence for the training of RBMs, and for
understanding the performance of deep architectures which utilize RBMs.
Revise this with your best effort: Hopfield networks (HNs) and Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are foundational models bridging statistical physics, machine learning, and neuroscience. Recent interest in their relationship stems from their shared formalism in statistical mechanics. While an exact mapping has been established for HNs with orthogonal (uncorrelated) patterns, we present a mapping for the more general and applicable case of correlated patterns. We demonstrate that any HN with *N* binary variables and *p*<*N* arbitrary binary patterns is equivalent to an RBM with *N* binary visible units and *p* Gaussian hidden units. We detail the conditions for reversibility and validate the approach on MNIST, where the mapped weights serve as an effective initialization for RBM training. This correspondence may enhance RBM training methods and inform our understanding of deep architectures built upon them.

input:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a powerful inductive bias for modelling
algorithmic reasoning procedures and data structures. Their prowess was mainly
demonstrated on tasks featuring Markovian dynamics, where querying any
associated data structure depends only on its latest state. For many tasks of
interest, however, it may be highly beneficial to support efficient data
structure queries dependent on previous states. This requires tracking the data
structure's evolution through time, placing significant pressure on the GNN's
latent representations. We introduce Persistent Message Passing (PMP), a
mechanism which endows GNNs with capability of querying past state by
explicitly persisting it: rather than overwriting node representations, it
creates new nodes whenever required. PMP generalises out-of-distribution to
more than 2x larger test inputs on dynamic temporal range queries,
significantly outperforming GNNs which overwrite states.
Revise this with your best effort:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a powerful inductive bias for modeling algorithmic reasoning and data structures. Their success has primarily been shown on tasks with Markovian dynamics, where querying a data structure depends only on its current state. Yet, for many important tasks, efficient queries may need to reference past states. This requires tracking a data structure’s evolution over time, placing substantial demands on the GNN’s latent representations.

We introduce Persistent Message Passing (PMP), a mechanism that enables GNNs to query prior states by explicitly preserving them: instead of overwriting node representations, PMP creates new nodes when necessary. This approach generalizes out-of-distribution to test inputs more than twice as large on dynamic temporal range queries, substantially outperforming GNNs that overwrite states.

input:
A deep equilibrium model uses implicit layers, which are implicitly defined
through an equilibrium point of an infinite sequence of computation. It avoids
any explicit computation of the infinite sequence by finding an equilibrium
point directly via root-finding and by computing gradients via implicit
differentiation. In this paper, we analyze the gradient dynamics of deep
equilibrium models with nonlinearity only on weight matrices and non-convex
objective functions of weights for regression and classification. Despite
non-convexity, convergence to global optimum at a linear rate is guaranteed
without any assumption on the width of the models, allowing the width to be
smaller than the output dimension and the number of data points. Moreover, we
prove a relation between the gradient dynamics of the deep implicit layer and
the dynamics of trust region Newton method of a shallow explicit layer. This
mathematically proven relation along with our numerical observation suggests
the importance of understanding implicit bias of implicit layers and an open
problem on the topic. Our proofs deal with implicit layers, weight tying and
nonlinearity on weights, and differ from those in the related literature.
Revise this with your best effort:
A deep equilibrium model employs implicit layers, defined by the equilibrium point of an infinite computational sequence. Rather than explicitly computing this sequence, it directly finds the equilibrium via root-finding and calculates gradients through implicit differentiation. This paper analyzes the gradient dynamics of such models featuring nonlinearity applied solely to weight matrices, under non-convex objective functions for regression and classification. Despite the non-convexity, we guarantee linear-rate convergence to a global optimum without requiring assumptions on model width—the width may be smaller than both the output dimension and the number of data points.

Furthermore, we establish a theoretical relationship between the gradient dynamics of this deep implicit layer and the dynamics of a trust-region Newton method applied to a shallow explicit layer. This proven connection, supported by numerical observations, highlights the importance of understanding the implicit bias inherent in such layers and points to a significant open problem in the field. Our proofs, which handle implicit layers, weight tying, and weight nonlinearity, are distinct from existing approaches in the related literature.

input:
The ability to learn continually without forgetting the past tasks is a
desired attribute for artificial learning systems. Existing approaches to
enable such learning in artificial neural networks usually rely on network
growth, importance based weight update or replay of old data from the memory.
In contrast, we propose a novel approach where a neural network learns new
tasks by taking gradient steps in the orthogonal direction to the gradient
subspaces deemed important for the past tasks. We find the bases of these
subspaces by analyzing network representations (activations) after learning
each task with Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in a single shot manner and
store them in the memory as Gradient Projection Memory (GPM). With qualitative
and quantitative analyses, we show that such orthogonal gradient descent
induces minimum to no interference with the past tasks, thereby mitigates
forgetting. We evaluate our algorithm on diverse image classification datasets
with short and long sequences of tasks and report better or on-par performance
compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.
Revise this with your best effort:
Continual learning—the ability to acquire new knowledge without erasing past skills—is a critical goal for artificial intelligence. Current methods for neural networks typically depend on expanding the network architecture, regulating weight updates by importance, or repeatedly rehearsing stored past data. We introduce a fundamentally different strategy: learning new tasks by taking gradient steps strictly orthogonal to the subspaces essential for previous tasks.

We identify these crucial subspaces in a single pass by applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to network activations after each task is learned, storing the resulting basis vectors in a compact Gradient Projection Memory (GPM). Both qualitative and quantitative analyses demonstrate that this orthogonal gradient descent creates minimal interference with prior knowledge, effectively preventing catastrophic forgetting.

Our algorithm is evaluated across diverse image classification datasets, using both short and long task sequences. It consistently matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance, offering a efficient and potent solution for continual learning.

input:
In high-dimensional state spaces, the usefulness of Reinforcement Learning
(RL) is limited by the problem of exploration. This issue has been addressed
using potential-based reward shaping (PB-RS) previously. In the present work,
we introduce Final-Volume-Preserving Reward Shaping (FV-RS). FV-RS relaxes the
strict optimality guarantees of PB-RS to a guarantee of preserved long-term
behavior. Being less restrictive, FV-RS allows for reward shaping functions
that are even better suited for improving the sample efficiency of RL
algorithms. In particular, we consider settings in which the agent has access
to an approximate plan. Here, we use examples of simulated robotic manipulation
tasks to demonstrate that plan-based FV-RS can indeed significantly improve the
sample efficiency of RL over plan-based PB-RS.
Revise this with your best effort: Reinforcement Learning (RL) struggles with exploration in complex, high-dimensional environments. While potential-based reward shaping (PB-RS) has addressed this with strict optimality guarantees, it can be overly restrictive. We propose Final-Volume-Preserving Reward Shaping (FV-RS), a novel method that relaxes these guarantees to preserve only long-term behavior. This flexibility allows for shaping functions better tailored to improving RL sample efficiency. We specifically examine settings where an agent has an approximate plan. Through simulated robotic manipulation tasks, we demonstrate that our plan-based FV-RS significantly outperforms plan-based PB-RS in sample efficiency.

input:
Many machine learning strategies designed to automate mathematical tasks
leverage neural networks to search large combinatorial spaces of mathematical
symbols. In contrast to traditional evolutionary approaches, using a neural
network at the core of the search allows learning higher-level symbolic
patterns, providing an informed direction to guide the search. When no labeled
data is available, such networks can still be trained using reinforcement
learning. However, we demonstrate that this approach can suffer from an early
commitment phenomenon and from initialization bias, both of which limit
exploration. We present two exploration methods to tackle these issues,
building upon ideas of entropy regularization and distribution initialization.
We show that these techniques can improve the performance, increase sample
efficiency, and lower the complexity of solutions for the task of symbolic
regression.
Revise this with your best effort: Many machine learning methods that automate mathematical work employ neural networks to explore vast combinatorial spaces of symbols. Unlike conventional evolutionary strategies, placing a neural network at the heart of the search enables it to learn higher-level symbolic patterns, offering a guided and informed direction. Even without labeled data, such networks can be trained via reinforcement learning. Yet, we show this approach is vulnerable to early commitment and initialization bias, which restrict exploration. To address these limitations, we introduce two exploration techniques based on entropy regularization and distribution initialization. These methods enhance performance, boost sample efficiency, and yield simpler solutions in symbolic regression tasks.

input:
We consider the problem of finding the best memoryless stochastic policy for
an infinite-horizon partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with
finite state and action spaces with respect to either the discounted or mean
reward criterion. We show that the (discounted) state-action frequencies and
the expected cumulative reward are rational functions of the policy, whereby
the degree is determined by the degree of partial observability. We then
describe the optimization problem as a linear optimization problem in the space
of feasible state-action frequencies subject to polynomial constraints that we
characterize explicitly. This allows us to address the combinatorial and
geometric complexity of the optimization problem using recent tools from
polynomial optimization. In particular, we estimate the number of critical
points and use the polynomial programming description of reward maximization to
solve a navigation problem in a grid world.
Revise this with your best effort:
We examine the task of identifying the optimal memoryless stochastic policy for a finite, infinite-horizon Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) under discounted or average reward criteria. Our analysis demonstrates that both the state-action frequencies and the expected cumulative reward are rational functions of the policy, with their degree governed by the level of partial observability. Consequently, the optimization can be reformulated as a linear program within the space of feasible state-action frequencies, subject to explicit polynomial constraints. This reformulation enables us to manage the problem's inherent combinatorial and geometric complexity using modern polynomial optimization techniques. As an application, we estimate the number of critical points and employ this polynomial programming framework to successfully solve a navigation task in a grid world.

*(Word count: 138)*

input:
Stochastic encoders have been used in rate-distortion theory and neural
compression because they can be easier to handle. However, in performance
comparisons with deterministic encoders they often do worse, suggesting that
noise in the encoding process may generally be a bad idea. It is poorly
understood if and when stochastic encoders do better than deterministic
encoders. In this paper we provide one illustrative example which shows that
stochastic encoders can significantly outperform the best deterministic
encoders. Our toy example suggests that stochastic encoders may be particularly
useful in the regime of "perfect perceptual quality".
Revise this with your best effort: Stochastic encoders are commonly employed in rate-distortion theory and neural compression due to their tractability. Yet, they typically underperform compared to deterministic encoders in benchmarks, implying that injecting noise may be generally detrimental. It remains unclear if and when stochastic encoders hold an advantage. Here, we present an illustrative example demonstrating that they can significantly outperform even the optimal deterministic encoder. This toy model indicates that stochastic encoders may be especially beneficial for achieving "perfect perceptual quality."

input:
We consider the problem of learned transform compression where we learn both,
the transform as well as the probability distribution over the discrete codes.
We utilize a soft relaxation of the quantization operation to allow for
back-propagation of gradients and employ vector (rather than scalar)
quantization of the latent codes. Furthermore, we apply similar relaxation in
the code probability assignments enabling direct optimization of the code
entropy. To the best of our knowledge, this approach is completely novel. We
conduct a set of proof-of concept experiments confirming the potency of our
approaches.
Revise this with your best effort: We address learned transform compression by jointly learning the transform and the discrete code distribution. To enable gradient back-propagation, we employ a soft relaxation of quantization and use vector—rather than scalar—quantization for the latent codes. A similar relaxation in code probability assignments allows direct optimization of code entropy. To our knowledge, this integrated approach is novel. Proof-of-concept experiments validate the effectiveness of our method.

input:
The dynamics of physical systems is often constrained to lower dimensional
sub-spaces due to the presence of conserved quantities. Here we propose a
method to learn and exploit such symmetry constraints building upon Hamiltonian
Neural Networks. By enforcing cyclic coordinates with appropriate loss
functions, we find that we can achieve improved accuracy on simple classical
dynamics tasks. By fitting analytic formulae to the latent variables in our
network we recover that our networks are utilizing conserved quantities such as
(angular) momentum.
Revise this with your best effort: The behavior of physical systems is often confined to lower-dimensional subspaces because of conserved quantities. We introduce a method to learn and exploit these symmetry constraints by enhancing Hamiltonian Neural Networks. By imposing cyclic coordinates through tailored loss functions, we achieve greater accuracy on classical dynamics tasks. Analytically fitting the network's latent variables reveals that it leverages conserved quantities like (angular) momentum.

input:
In this work, we study the behavior of standard models for community
detection under spectral manipulations. Through various ablation experiments,
we evaluate the impact of bandpass filtering on the performance of a GCN: we
empirically show that most of the necessary and used information for nodes
classification is contained in the low-frequency domain, and thus contrary to
images, high frequencies are less crucial to community detection. In
particular, it is sometimes possible to obtain accuracies at a state-of-the-art
level with simple classifiers that rely only on a few low frequencies.
Revise this with your best effort: In this study, we examine how standard community detection models respond to spectral manipulations. Using ablation experiments, we assess the effect of bandpass filtering on a Graph Convolutional Network's performance. Our findings show that, unlike in image processing, the high-frequency domain is less critical for node classification. Most essential information resides in low frequencies. Consequently, simple classifiers using only a few low frequencies can sometimes achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.

input:
We propose a new framework of synthesizing data using deep generative models
in a differentially private manner. Within our framework, sensitive data are
sanitized with rigorous privacy guarantees in a one-shot fashion, such that
training deep generative models is possible without re-using the original data.
Hence, no extra privacy costs or model constraints are incurred, in contrast to
popular approaches such as Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
(DP-SGD), which, among other issues, causes degradation in privacy guarantees
as the training iteration increases. We demonstrate a realization of our
framework by making use of the characteristic function and an adversarial
re-weighting objective, which are of independent interest as well. Our proposal
has theoretical guarantees of performance, and empirical evaluations on
multiple datasets show that our approach outperforms other methods at
reasonable levels of privacy.
Revise this with your best effort: We propose a framework for synthesizing data with deep generative models under differential privacy. In our approach, sensitive data is sanitized once with rigorous privacy guarantees, enabling model training without further access to the original data. This eliminates the accumulating privacy costs and performance constraints typical of iterative methods like Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD). We implement the framework using a characteristic function and an adversarial re-weighting objective—techniques that are also of independent interest. Theoretically grounded, our method demonstrates strong empirical performance across multiple datasets, outperforming alternatives at practical privacy levels.

input:
Self-supervised visual representation learning aims to learn useful
